passage:
Thursday. After a brutal appraisal, Alka walked out of the office and bought a pack of cigarettes from the kiosk she had avoided for four months. She smoked two behind the parking lot.
Friday. She woke with the pack on her bedside table and a voice in her head: You've already blown it. Four months, gone. Might as well finish the pack and stop pretending.
Then she remembered a line from the cessation clinic: "When it says you've failed, that's shame talking, not the truth." She said it out loud to the empty room. Before lunch she called Jasleen, her friend who had quit two years earlier. "I smoked yesterday. I want to throw the whole thing away. Talk me down?"
"Proud of you for calling," Jasleen said. "Bin the pack while I'm on the phone."
Monday. Alka kept her clinic appointment and told the counsellor everything. Day one again, but with four months of knowing how.

qa.q: How long had Alka avoided the kiosk?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: Why did the thought "Might as well finish the pack" feel so convincing to Alka on Friday?
qa.a: After one slip it felt as if all four months were already gone, so shame made giving up completely look like the honest choice.

qa.q: What kept Alka's slip from becoming a full return?
qa.a: She named the thought as shame talking, not the truth, and called Jasleen the same day, then kept her clinic appointment.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel getting Alka's call?
qa.a: Jasleen, who quit two years earlier, likely understands the pull well and feels glad that Alka reached out instead of hiding.

grounding: Shows a young woman after a smoking lapse feeling the pull to give up entirely, naming it as shame and calling a support person that day.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Actor]
passage:
Eshaan, shut the cabin door. People here think Chinmay from Accounts has always had it together. Not quite.
You told me yesterday you slipped last weekend and now you're thinking, what's the point. I know that voice. At twenty-five I had been off alcohol for five months when my engagement broke. That night I drank alone in my room. Next morning the voice was very clear: You're a drunk. Always were. Why bother now? And it made a horrible sort of sense.
I was halfway to the liquor shop again when I remembered my counsellor saying that shame always argues for giving up. I stood on the pavement and said under my breath, "That's shame talking." Then I called my sister, right there, outside the shop. She came in an auto within half an hour. I didn't drink that day, or the next.
So. Your slip was last weekend. Who are you calling today? Not next week. Today.

qa.q: What happened to Chinmay's engagement?
qa.a: It broke, after five months off alcohol.

qa.q: Why did the voice's words make 'a horrible sort of sense' to Chinmay?
qa.a: After drinking alone, shame made the slip feel like proof of being 'a drunk', so giving up seemed logical in that moment.

qa.q: What does Chinmay urge Eshaan to do, and why today?
qa.a: Call a support person today, not next week, because naming the voice as shame and reaching someone quickly keeps a slip from becoming a return.

qa.q: What might the sister have felt getting the call from outside the shop?
qa.a: She was likely frightened, but coming by auto within half an hour shows she chose to show up without judgement.

grounding: Illustrates, through a colleague's memory, the pull to give up after a lapse, recognised as shame, and calling a support person the same day.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Actor]
passage:
Diary, Sunday night
I used today. After four months. I don't even want to write it.
The first thing I thought was: that's it, I've failed, so I might as well keep going. I actually started planning where to get more. That thought felt so reasonable.
Then I remembered what the group says: when you hear "you've already failed," that's shame talking, not truth.
So at 9 p.m. I called Sunaina from the group. I cried. She said, "One slip isn't a return unless you let shame drive. Come to the morning meeting."
I'm going. Four months still happened.
Sarika

qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What was Sarika's first thought after the lapse?
qa.a: Sarika felt ashamed and hopeless, thinking the failure meant there was no point stopping now.

qa.q: What turning point kept the slip from becoming a return?
qa.a: Recognising the thought as shame talking and calling Sunaina that same night, then planning the morning meeting.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel after the call?
qa.a: Sunaina is probably concerned but encouraging, glad Sarika reached out the same day.

grounding: Shows a young person after a lapse feeling the pull to give up, recognising it as shame, and calling a support person that day.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Actor]
passage:
In Dehradun, the morning after her lapse, Charu sat on the steps of the temple near her house. After five months without pills, she'd taken them again at a friend's place.
The thought came clear and cold: You've already failed. Why stop now?
She almost believed it. She'd started thinking about who else might have some.
Then she remembered her counsellor's words: "When the voice says it's over, that's shame, not truth." She took out her phone and called her brother.
"Pradeep bhaiya, I slipped last night."
A pause. "Thank you for telling me, Charu. Where are you? I'm coming. We'll call your counsellor together."
Charu waited on the steps, still shaking, but not alone.

qa.q: Where did Charu sit the morning after her lapse?
qa.a: On the steps of the temple near her house.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when the thought "You've already failed" came?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and tempted to give up completely, almost believing the lapse was the end.

qa.q: What turning point did Charu choose?
qa.a: She recognised the thought as shame, called her brother that day, and planned to call her counsellor with him.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be feeling when Charu calls?
qa.a: Pradeep is probably worried but calm and grateful she told him, focusing on coming to her.

grounding: Shows a young woman after a lapse feeling the pull to give up, recognising it as shame, and calling her brother that day.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Actor]
passage: The morning after the office party in Lisbon, Sofia woke with a dry mouth and the memory of wine she had promised herself she would never drink again. A hundred and forty days, gone. She sat on the edge of the bed. The thought came smooth and reasonable: You've already failed. Might as well stop pretending. There was a bottle shop two streets away that opened at ten. She noticed how kind the thought sounded, and how much it felt like the voice that had kept her drinking alone for years. That's shame talking, she remembered Elif saying at group. She picked up the phone. "Elif, I drank last night. And this morning I want to give up." "Thank you for calling," Elif said. "Meet me at the café at ten, not the shop. We'll call your counsellor together."

qa.q: How many days had Sofia gone without drinking before the party?
qa.a: A hundred and forty days.

qa.q: Why does the thought "You've already failed" feel so tempting to Sofia?
qa.a: She feels ashamed after the lapse, and the thought sounds reasonable and kind, offering an end to that painful feeling.

qa.q: What stopped the slip from becoming a return?
qa.a: Sofia recognised the thought as shame talking and called Elif that same morning, agreeing to meet and call the counsellor.

qa.q: What is it like for Elif to get Sofia's call?
qa.a: Elif seems glad to be trusted and steady, thanking Sofia and turning the morning toward help instead of the shop.
